title: Part I: Bricks, Beads and Bones: The Harappan Civilisation

topics.title: Harappan civilisation: names, culture and sites

learn.hook: Over 4,500 years ago, people from the Indus plains to Gujarat were using the same kind of bricks, seals and weights. How do we even name a world that left no readable writing?
points: The Indus valley civilisation is also called the Harappan civilisation, after Harappa, the first site where it was discovered.

In archaeology, a 'culture' means a group of objects of a distinctive style, usually found together within a specific geographical area and period of time. Harappan seals, beads, weights and stone blades form such a group.
The Mature Harappan phase is dated c. 2600–1900 BCE. Cultures before it in the same area are called Early Harappan; those after it are called Late Harappan.

Early Harappan settlements were generally small, had distinctive pottery, agriculture and pastoralism, and some crafts. A break between early and mature phases is shown by large-scale burning at some sites and abandonment of certain settlements.

Key sites: Harappa and Mohenjodaro (now in Pakistan), Dholavira and Lothal (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Rakhigarhi and Banawali (Haryana), Chanhudaro (Sindh), Nageshwar (Gujarat coast), Balakot (Baluchistan coast) and Shortughai (Afghanistan).

example.q: A student finds burnt layers at a site lying between Early Harappan pottery below and Mature Harappan seals above. What does this suggest?
steps: Lower layers are older; upper layers are younger.
Early Harappan material lies below, so it came first.
Burnt layers between them point to destruction or a break.
This matches the break seen at some sites before the mature phase.
example.answer: There was a break, possibly with burning and abandonment, between the Early Harappan and Mature Harappan phases at that site.

learn.reallife: Dholavira in Kutch, Gujarat, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, so a Harappan city is now as much a part of India's heritage list as the Taj Mahal.

learn.hook: A burnt grain of barley, smaller than a grain of rice, can tell us what was cooked in a Mohenjodaro kitchen 4,500 years ago.
points: Harappans ate a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct diet from charred grains and seeds studied by archaeo-botanists.
Grains found include wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame. Millets are found at sites in Gujarat. Finds of rice are relatively rare.
Animal bones include cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig; studies by archaeo-zoologists show these were domesticated.
Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial are also found. We do not know if Harappans hunted these themselves or got the meat from other hunting communities.
Bones of fish and fowl are found as well, so food came from farmers, herders, fisherfolk and possibly hunter-gatherers.

example.answer: Peasants, pastoralists, fisherfolk and hunter-gatherers (or communities trading meat).

learn.hook: At Kalibangan, archaeologists found a field ploughed nearly 5,000 years ago, with furrows still visible. A farmer in Rajasthan today might recognise the pattern!
points: Seals and terracotta sculptures show the bull was known, so oxen were probably used for ploughing.
Terracotta models of the plough have been found at sites in Cholistan and at Banawali (Haryana).

At Kalibangan (Rajasthan), a ploughed field was found, associated with Early Harappan levels. It had two sets of furrows at right angles to each other, suggesting two different crops were grown together.

Irrigation was probably needed as most Harappan sites lie in semi-arid lands. Traces of canals were found at Shortughai (Afghanistan), but not in Punjab or Sindh. Water from wells and water reservoirs at Dholavira (Gujarat) was also used.
For harvesting, Harappans may have used stone blades set in wooden handles, or metal tools; archaeologists are still not sure.

example.q: Why do furrows at right angles in the Kalibangan field suggest two crops were grown together?
steps: One set of furrows can be used for one crop.
A second set at right angles creates a grid.
Two crops sown in different directions in one field is a known practice.
So the pattern hints at mixed cropping.
example.answer: Criss-crossing furrows suggest that two different crops were grown in the same field at the same time.

learn.reallife: Rajasthan farmers still grow mustard and gram together in one field; the Kalibangan furrows hint that mixed cropping is a very old Indian practice.

topics.title: Mohenjodaro: a planned city and its drains

learn.hook: Many Indian cities still struggle with waterlogged streets in the monsoon. Mohenjodaro had covered street drains about 4,500 years ago!
points: Mohenjodaro was divided into two parts: a smaller but higher Citadel (to the west) and a much larger but lower Lower Town (to the east). The Citadel was walled, and so was the Lower Town.
Buildings were built on platforms, which served as foundations. This means the settlement was planned first and then built. Platforms needed an enormous amount of labour.
Bricks, sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio: length four times the height and breadth twice the height (4:2:1). This ratio was used across Harappan settlements.
Streets were laid out in an approximately grid pattern, intersecting at right angles. Drains seem to have been laid out first, and houses built along them.
House drains, carrying waste water, were connected to street drains. Long drainage channels had sumps at intervals for cleaning. Drainage systems are found in smaller settlements too, such as Lothal.

example.q: A Harappan brick is 10 cm high. Using the standard ratio, what are its breadth and length?
steps: Ratio length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1.
Breadth = 2 × 10 = 20 cm.
Length = 4 × 10 = 40 cm.

learn.reallife: Smart City projects in India stress planned drainage first. Mohenjodaro's planners seem to have done that long ago: drains first, houses next.

topics.title: Houses, the Citadel and the Great Bath

learn.hook: Imagine a house in Mohenjodaro: you walk in from a lane but cannot see the courtyard from the doorway. Privacy mattered even 4,500 years ago!
points: Many Lower Town houses were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides. The courtyard was probably used for cooking and weaving, especially in hot and dry weather.
There were no windows in walls along the ground level, and the main entrance did not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard, which suggests concern for privacy.

Every house had its own bathroom paved with bricks, with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. Some houses had staircases to a second storey or roof. Many houses had wells; Mohenjodaro had about 700 wells.
The Citadel had structures probably used for special public purposes, like the warehouse (only lower brick portions survive; upper wooden parts decayed) and the Great Bath.

The Great Bath was a large rectangular tank in a courtyard with a corridor on all four sides, two flights of steps on the north and south, bricks set on edge with gypsum mortar to make it watertight. Its uniqueness and location suggest a special ritual bath.

example.q: Give two reasons why scholars think the Great Bath had a special, perhaps ritual, purpose.
steps: It is a unique structure, not found elsewhere in that form.
It stands in the Citadel, among public buildings.
It had careful watertight construction and side rooms, one with a large well.
example.answer: Its unique design and its location in the Citadel with other special buildings suggest a ritual bath.

learn.reallife: The idea of a sacred tank survives across India, from temple tanks (kalyani or pushkarini) in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu to ghats on the Ganga.

learn.hook: In Egypt, pharaohs were buried with mountains of gold. What did Harappans place in their graves, and what does that tell us?
points: Archaeologists study burials and artefacts to find social or economic differences.

At Harappan burial sites the dead were generally laid in pits. Some pits were lined with bricks. Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps showing a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.

Jewellery is found in burials of both men and women. In one Harappa burial (excavated in the 1980s), a man had an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads. Some burials had copper mirrors.
Overall, Harappans do not seem to have believed in burying precious things with the dead, so burial differences are not very sharp.

Artefacts are classified as utilitarian (daily-use objects like querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers, made of stone or clay, found everywhere) or luxuries (rare objects of costly non-local materials or complicated technology, such as little faience pots). Faience vessels are found in large cities like Mohenjodaro and Harappa but not in small ones like Kalibangan. Gold was rare and found in hoards.

example.q: A grave has a brick-lined pit with pottery, while another has a plain pit with nothing. What can a historian infer, and what caution is needed?
steps: Brick lining and goods mean more effort and resources.
This hints at differences in status.
But Harappan graves rarely have precious items.
So differences existed but were not extreme.
example.answer: There were some social differences, but the evidence does not show sharp inequality like that in Egyptian royal burials.

learn.hook: A red carnelian bead from the Indus could end up in a royal grave in Mesopotamia. Its journey began at a tiny town called Chanhudaro.
points: Chanhudaro was a tiny settlement (less than 7 hectares) almost exclusively devoted to craft production: bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.
Bead materials: stones like carnelian (beautiful red), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals like copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta (burnt clay).
Beads were made in many shapes: disc, cylindrical, spherical, barrel and segmented. Some were decorated by incising or painting, some had etched designs.

Techniques: nodules were chipped into rough shapes, then flaked into final form; grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process. The red colour of carnelian came from firing the yellowish raw material and beads at various stages. Specialised drills have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

To identify a production centre, archaeologists look for raw material (stone nodules, whole shells, copper ore), tools, unfinished objects, rejects and waste material. Waste is one of the best indicators.

example.q: An excavator finds shell pieces with cut marks, broken bangles and whole shells in one area. Is it a craft workshop?
steps: Whole shells = raw material.
Pieces with cut marks = waste.
Broken bangles = rejects/unfinished objects.
All three together point to production on the spot.
example.answer: Yes, it was probably a shell-working centre, because raw material, waste and unfinished objects are found together.

learn.hook: Copper from Rajasthan, gold from the south, blue lapis lazuli from Afghanistan: Harappan craftspeople ran a supply chain long before trucks and railways.
points: Harappans got raw materials in many ways. Bullock carts carried goods over land; riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries and coastal routes were probably also used. Terracotta toy models of bullock carts have been found.

One strategy was to set up settlements near sources: Nageshwar and Balakot near shell sources; Shortughai in far Afghanistan near lapis lazuli (a blue stone); Lothal near carnelian (from Bharuch, Gujarat), steatite (south Rajasthan and north Gujarat) and metal (Rajasthan).
Nageshwar and Balakot specialised in making shell objects such as bangles, ladles and inlay, which were sent to other settlements.
Another strategy was sending expeditions: to the Khetri region of Rajasthan for copper and to South India for gold.

In the Khetri area, archaeologists found evidence of the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture, with distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects. Its people may have supplied copper to the Harappans.

example.q: Why would the Harappans set up Shortughai so far away in Afghanistan?
steps: Shortughai lies near sources of lapis lazuli.

example.answer: To secure a steady supply of lapis lazuli from close to its source.

learn.hook: Your online parcel has a barcode; a Harappan sack of goods had a clay sealing. Both said: 'Untouched, from the right sender!'
points: Seals and sealings were used to facilitate long-distance communication. A sack of goods was tied with rope, the knot covered with wet clay, and seals pressed on it. The impression is called a sealing; an intact sealing showed the goods were not tampered with and identified the sender.
The Harappan seal is typically made of steatite (a stone). It often has an animal motif and signs from a script that remains undeciphered.
The script was probably not alphabetic, because it has too many signs: somewhere between 375 and 400. It was written from right to left (wider spacing on the right, cramped on the left).
Inscriptions are short; the longest has about 26 signs. Writing appears on seals, copper tools, rims of jars, copper and terracotta tablets, jewellery, bone rods and even an ancient signboard.

Weights were usually cubical, made of chert, with no markings. Lower denominations were binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … up to 12,800), while higher denominations followed the decimal system. Smaller weights were probably for jewellery and beads; metal scale-pans have been found.

example.q: In the binary series 1, 2, 4, 8, …, what are the next three weights after 8?
steps: Each weight is double the previous one.

topics.title: Ancient authority: who ruled the Harappans?

learn.hook: Same brick ratio from Punjab to Gujarat, same weights, planned cities. Who made all these decisions? Historians still argue!
points: Signs of complex decisions: extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts (pottery, seals, weights, bricks); bricks of standard ratio even though not produced in a single centre; planned settlements; craft production organised in places near raw materials.
Palace and king? A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace by archaeologists, but no spectacular finds were associated with it.

A stone statue was labelled 'priest-king' because archaeologists were familiar with Mesopotamian history and its 'priest-kings'. Harappan ritual practices are not yet understood, so we cannot know if those who performed them held political power.

Theories: (1) there were no rulers and everybody enjoyed equal status; (2) there was no single ruler but several, such as one each for Mohenjodaro and Harappa; (3) these were part of a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, planned settlements, standard bricks and settlements near raw material sources.
As things stand, the last theory seems the most plausible, as it is unlikely entire communities could have collectively made and implemented such complex decisions.

steps: Bricks were made in many places, not in one factory.

This fits best with a single state.
example.answer: It supports the single-state theory, since a common authority could enforce such standards.

learn.hook: Imagine a city where people stopped using writing, seals and standard weights within a few generations. That is roughly what happened after c. 1900 BCE.
points: By c. 1800 BCE most Mature Harappan sites in regions such as Cholistan had been abandoned.
At the same time, population expanded into new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

In the few Harappan sites that continued to be occupied after 1900 BCE, material culture changed: distinctive artefacts such as weights, seals and special beads disappeared; writing, long-distance trade and craft specialisation also disappeared. House construction techniques deteriorated and large public structures were no longer built. These are called Late Harappan or 'successor' cultures, and show a rural way of life.
Suggested causes include climatic change, deforestation, excessive floods, the shifting and/or drying up of rivers, and overuse of the landscape.

These causes may explain the end of some settlements but not the collapse of a whole civilisation. One explanation is the disappearance of a strong unifying element, perhaps the Harappan state, shown by the vanishing of seals, the script, distinctive beads and pottery.

example.q: Why is 'floods' alone not a convincing explanation for the end of the entire Harappan civilisation?
steps: Floods could ruin settlements near rivers.

So a wider explanation, like the collapse of a unifying state, is suggested.

learn.hook: Alexander Cunningham held a Harappan seal in his hands in the 1870s but could not tell how old it was. The discovery waited another 50 years!
points: Alexander Cunningham, the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), began excavations in the mid-nineteenth century. He used accounts of Chinese Buddhist pilgrims (4th–7th centuries CE) to locate early settlements; his main interest was the Early Historic period.
Harappa did not fit his framework. An Englishman gave him a Harappan seal; he tried to place it in a familiar time-frame and failed to realise how old Harappa was (Report on Harappan seal, 1875).

In the early twentieth century, Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa in layers much older than Early Historic levels; R.D. Banerji found similar seals at Mohenjodaro. In 1924 John Marshall, Director-General of the ASI, announced the discovery of a new civilisation in the Indus valley.

Marshall excavated along regular horizontal units measured uniformly throughout the mound, ignoring the site's stratigraphy. So artefacts from different layers were grouped together and their context was lost.

R.E.M. Wheeler, Director-General of the ASI from 1944, corrected this by following the stratigraphy of the mound. Later landmarks: Wheeler at Harappa (1946), S.R. Rao at Lothal (1955), B.B. Lal and B.K. Thapar at Kalibangan (1960), R.S. Bisht at Dholavira (1990).

example.q: Why was Marshall's method a problem?
steps: A mound has layers formed at different times (stratigraphy).
Marshall dug in uniform horizontal units regardless of layers.
Objects from different layers got mixed in one unit.
So their date and context were lost.
example.answer: Ignoring stratigraphy mixed up artefacts of different periods, destroying valuable information about context.

learn.reallife: The ASI, founded in Cunningham's time, still protects over 3,600 monuments across India, from Dholavira to the Red Fort.

topics.title: New sites and the problems of interpretation

learn.hook: A small clay figure of a woman with heavy jewellery: is she a goddess, a toy or a household charm? Archaeologists must decide with no label attached!
points: After Partition (1947) the major sites Harappa and Mohenjodaro were in Pakistan. Indian archaeologists explored new areas: surveys in Kutch, Punjab and Haryana added many sites, with Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira excavated in India. Explorations continued in Pakistan too.

New techniques and questions: scientific analysis of materials, and studies of plant and animal remains, are used to understand diet, trade and environment; since the 1980s there has been growing international interest.

Classifying finds is a basic step: by material (stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory) and by function. Function is hard to know; archaeologists often compare with present-day objects (e.g. querns) or study the context of the find.

Religion is inferred from objects: terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled with elaborate head-dresses, were called 'mother goddesses'; rare stone statues of men seated in a standard posture were labelled 'priest-king'; fire altars are reported from Kalibangan and Lothal; seals show a 'unicorn' and a figure seated cross-legged in a 'yogic' posture surrounded by animals, regarded as 'proto-Shiva'; conical stones have been classified as lingas.

Such interpretations often use later traditions. For example, Rudra appears in the Rigveda, but he is not depicted there as Pashupati or as a yogi. So using later texts to explain Harappan objects has limits.

example.q: Why is the 'proto-Shiva' identification of the yogic figure on a seal debated?
steps: The identification relies on later Hindu ideas of Shiva as Pashupati and yogi.
The Rigveda, an earlier text, mentions Rudra.
But Rudra in the Rigveda is not shown as Pashupati or as a yogi.
So the link between the seal and later Shiva is uncertain.
example.answer: Because it projects later religious ideas backwards; even the Rigveda's Rudra does not match the image.
